title: Hash Functions
summary: Turning keys into numbers - what a hash function must and should do, from keys to bucket indexes, why naive hashes cluster, polynomial string hashing, FNV-1a, std::hash and how to hash your own types, combining hashes, collisions and the birthday paradox, and hash flooding attacks.

cards.q: Which property is required (not just desirable) of a hash function?
cards.a:
Equal keys always produce equal hashes

If equal keys could hash differently, lookups would search the wrong bucket. Different keys sharing a hash is allowed.

cards.q: Why is hashing a point as hash(x) ^ hash(y) a poor choice?
cards.a:
(1, 2) and (2, 1) collide, and x == y gives 0

XOR is symmetric and cancels equal values, so structured keys collide a lot.

cards.q: With 365 buckets, about how many random keys until the first collision is likely?
cards.a:
about 23

The birthday paradox: about the square root of the bucket count.
